deep.reconstruction:
The page is a table of experimental physics data, not a mathematical derivation. Title: 'Schwingungen des verkehrten Pendels – Stehend' (oscillations of the inverted pendulum, standing position).

Columns:
1. Date and time of day (V = Vormittag, morning; N = Nachmittag, afternoon).
2. 'Barom.' – barometer reading in Paris measure. The first entry 27'' 6'''.9 means 27 inches 6.9 lines; later entries give only the lines.
3. 'Th. Cent.' – temperature in °C.
4. '200 D.Sch.' – time in seconds for 200 Doppelschwingungen (double oscillations).
5. 'Eine D.S.' – period of one double oscillation, T.

Computation on the page (the only one): T = t_200/200.
- 1351.2/200 = 6.7560
- 1358.2/200 = 6.7910
- 1345.44/200 = 6.7272
- 1341.0/200 = 6.7050
- 1336.4/200 = 6.6820
- 1339.06/200 = 6.6953
- 1337.2/200 = 6.6860
- 1336.54/200 = 6.6827
- 1367.35/200 = 6.83675, written 6.8367, with a '?' in the margin
- 1367.31/200 = 6.83655, written 6.8365

The later rows (1830 Jul 30, Aug 1; 1831 Jan 21 twice; 1846 Apr 29) give only the number of double oscillations observed ('aus 157(?)', 125, 192, 175, 80). So T was derived from shorter series, and the raw times are not recorded.

Purpose (my interpretation): the data show a strong, monotone temperature dependence of the period, ranging from T ≈ 6.40 s at −0.6 °C to 6.90 s at 24.6 °C. That is what one expects of an inverted pendulum near its stability limit. Its restoring torque is (elastic torque of the spring or suspension) minus m g l, and the elastic part decreases with temperature.

My own check, not on the page: 1/T² is very nearly linear in temperature.
- 1/6.4010² = 0.024406
- 1/6.6827² = 0.022392
- 1/6.9008² = 0.020999
- Slopes: −1.34e−4 per °C between −0.6 and 14.4 °C, and −1.37e−4 per °C between 14.4 and 24.6 °C.

So the effective stiffness (∝ 1/T²) falls linearly with temperature. This is consistent with a linear thermoelastic coefficient of the spring, amplified by the near-cancellation with gravity. No fit or reduction formula is written on the page. The barometer column is presumably recorded for possible buoyancy or air-resistance corrections. The 1846 entry (7.194 s, temperature only '+') shows the instrument was revisited 16 years later.
errors: No arithmetic errors in the divisions shown. Row 29 N: 1367.35/200 = 6.83675 is written 6.8367 (truncated rather than rounded up); Gauss himself put a '?' beside this row.
Aug 1 entry: last digit overwritten (6.9008 or 6.9009); cannot be checked because the raw time is not recorded.

The Jun 3 and Jun 7 periods (6.756 at 18.2 °C, 6.791 at 19.4 °C) lie somewhat above the trend of the other June data (implied slope ≈ 0.029 s/°C versus ≈ 0.015–0.02 s/°C elsewhere). This is scatter in the observations, not a computational slip.

results.what: Period of an inverted (spring-stabilized) pendulum measured as total time of 200 double oscillations divided by 200, recorded with temperature and pressure
results.modern_name: Experimental determination of oscillation period; temperature dependence of an inverted pendulum / elastic restoring force
results.usually_credited_to: Inverted pendula as sensitive instruments were used by various 19th-century physicists; no specific priority question attaches to this data

results.what: Data implicitly showing that 1/T^2 (effective stiffness) decreases linearly with temperature (my observation, not stated by Gauss)
results.modern_name: Thermoelastic coefficient of a spring (temperature dependence of elastic modulus), amplified in an inverted pendulum
results.usually_credited_to: Thermoelastic effects on springs studied by many (e.g. Kupffer, Wertheim, mid-19th c.)

deep.surprise_reason: A routine laboratory log of pendulum periods with simple divisions by 200; no mathematical content beyond arithmetic. Gauss's experimental physics activity in Göttingen (around 1830, shortly before his collaboration with Weber) is well known. The only mild interest is the instrument and its long-term (1830–1846) monitoring.

checkable.asserts: both ≈ 1.34e-4 to 1.37e-4 per °C, i.e. 1/T^2 is nearly linear in temperature

transcription_corrections: 'Th. Cent' is 'Th. Cent.' (Thermometer Centigrade); '27² 6'9' means 27 Paris inches 6.9 lines (27'' 6'''.9).
'200 D. Sch.' = 200 Doppelschwingungen; 'Eine D. S.' = one Doppelschwingung.
Jun 29 row: date written over a correction ('29 N'); the '?' at the right margin belongs to the period 6.8367.
Jul 30 row: count 'aus 15?' – last digit overwritten (possibly 157 or 150); Aug 1 period last digit overwritten (6.9008/6.9009).
1831 month reads 'Januar' (abbreviated 'Jan.'); the 1846 row has only '+' in the temperature column and no barometer value.
